body:
Nick Halloway wrote:
> 
> The funny thing about people who so passionately exclude opposing views
> is that they probably do so partly because they really haven't examined
> them themselves.  So they are prey to sudden conversions.  We may expect
> Pyro soon to become a passionate Maoist.  They will turn around suddenly,
> and suddenly there is a new Right/Wrong coloring to their world.

	Yes.  As I recall, on of the things that got Hoffer going was the
success of the Communist secret police in absorbing the operatives of
the Gestapo (and related organs) after World War II.  Ideologically, one
would think this astonishing.  Hoffer thought it meant that the
Communists simply offered the only outlet available for people of a
fanatical mindset.

> I think that thinking this way is one thing that happens when people take
> on a dissident view, feeling like a minority in a large society.  They do
> not have enough social support to make them feel comfortable in a
> different view.  I've noticed that people really deny the power
> to influence that advertising and the media have.  But the modern media --
> including the internet!  permeate people's lives with certain viewpoints.
> When they are barraged with mainstream viewpoints or ones profoundly
> different from their own, without the luxury of choosing what they're
> exposed to, and without the time to assimilate, they get defensive and
> close down.  Probably people who are not massively exposed to media
> would be more relaxed about their own views.  What is natural to humans
> is to associate mostly with friends, whose views we are familiar with and
> who we've found to be congenial to us.  Not to constantly have to deal
> with the opinions of strangers about what we think.
> Also "rigid thinkers" may be rebelling and their views have a psychological
> meaning of rebellion; symbolic, verbal rebellion, so that disagreement
> has a heavy meaning for them.

	Somee of my favorite lines on this come from a bit of contemporary
music.  One is just, "Allies, in a world of too much choice."  The other
is "If faith is blind, through darkness it shall guide us."

	Before it gets lost in all the criticism, I'd point out that the last
line tells one about the virtuous possibilities of zealotry.  There
really are times when confusion and danger overwhelm us, and blind faith
can be the only thing that gives anyone direction.  Fortunately, those
occasions are rare.  Unfortunately, the human capacity to face them
sometimes becomes a need so powerful that, in the words of ISAIF, "If
our society had no social problems at all, the leftists (and here we may
insert, 'any zealot') would have to INVENT problems..."

Scott
